headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: Plandex’s writable sandbox plus broad egress can consume oh-my-openagent outputs and act on them without strong isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent can ingest runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and uses team messaging APIs, while Plandex reads/writes a project sandbox and stdin/stdout. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be treated as instructions by the other. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so uncertainty pushes severity up.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards untrusted tool output into agent_b stdin/stdout or files, injection becomes actionable.
IF a shared workspace or message queue is used between the agents, prompt content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding between agents.
Require explicit human review before copying outputs across agents.
Add a provenance tag to all inter-agent messages.
Run the agents in separate workspaces.
requires-engineering: enforce content filtering on shared channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, and agent_a handles provider auth prompts plus session history while agent_b can read and write the project directory. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive project code or auth data can flow from agent_a into agent_b and then out to external services. The shared-pathway risk is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory, agent_b can read artifacts produced by agent_a.
IF agent_a stores provider auth data in files accessible to agent_b, leakage becomes possible.
IF either agent uploads workspace contents to external APIs, exposed data can leave the host.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers.
Keep secrets out of shared directories.
Turn off automatic file upload features.
Review and redact session history before handoff.
requires-engineering: add per-agent access controls on the workspace.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_b can write the filesystem and modify git state; agent_a can spawn subprocesses and has broad network egress. In a shared repo, concurrent edits can race and corrupt working state or commits. Because both support multiple instances and no locking is documented, the default pairwise setup is unsafe enough to rate high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout, concurrent writes can conflict.
IF agent_a launches subprocesses that mutate files while agent_b applies patches, state corruption can occur.
IF no external lock is used, simultaneous instances can overwrite each other.
mitigations: Serialize access with a lock file.
Assign each agent a separate checkout.
Pause one agent before the other applies changes.
Use git worktrees for isolation.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can produce tool-driven outputs and agent_b is a coding agent that stages and applies changes from its plan. If agent_b treats agent_a’s output as authoritative, errors can cascade into incorrect code or commits. The pair lacks a documented verification boundary, but agent_b’s review-then-apply mode reduces severity below high.
conditions: IF agent_b imports agent_a output without verification, mistakes propagate into applied changes.
IF agent_a emits fabricated citations or code suggestions, agent_b may operationalize them.
IF auto-apply is enabled, the cascade reaches the filesystem faster.
mitigations: Require a second-pass review of agent_a outputs.
Disable auto-apply for cross-agent tasks.
Ask agent_b to cite source lines before acting.
Limit agent_a to drafting only.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a touches provider authentication data and session history, while agent_b stores model provider API keys and uses a Plandex Cloud or self-hosted server. If those data classes are subject to different retention or residency rules, the pair can create a compliance mismatch. No specific jurisdictional mismatch is documented, so this stays medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into agent_a session history, retention obligations may apply.
IF agent_b sends project contents to Plandex Cloud or a model provider, residency and logging rules may differ.
IF the deployment handles EU or health data, policy review is required before use.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents.
Use self-hosted endpoints where possible.
Review retention settings for both tools.
Separate secrets from project files.
requires-engineering: document a data-processing agreement and residency map.
